title: Concurrency
note: When threads share memory, the order of their steps is unpredictable, so any read–modify–write on shared data needs synchronization. Deadlock needs four conditions at once (the Coffman conditions): mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Break any one and deadlock cannot occur.

read.title: Two threads, one counter
text: Imagine two threads each adding one to a shared counter a million times. The total should be two million, but it usually comes out lower. The line count++ is really three steps: read the value, add one, write it back. If both threads read 41 before either writes, both write 42 and one increment is lost. That is a race condition, and it appears only under certain timing, which makes it hard to reproduce.

The fix is to make the read–modify–write indivisible, either with an atomic instruction or by guarding it with a mutex so only one thread is in that critical section at a time. Locks bring their own hazard. If thread A holds lock 1 and waits for lock 2 while thread B holds lock 2 and waits for lock 1, neither can proceed. Deadlock needs all four Coffman conditions, so the common cure is to break circular wait by always acquiring locks in the same global order.
Async code avoids many of these problems by running callbacks on a single thread, but it trades them for others. One long, blocking computation freezes every other task waiting in the event loop.

q.q: Why does the shared counter come out too low?
o: Increments are lost when both threads read before writing

q.q: What common cure for deadlock does the reading describe?
o: Acquiring locks in one global order

q.q: What is the main hazard of async code named in the reading?
o: A blocking computation freezing other tasks
